claim: The adaptive traffic signal system operates through a decentralized gradient descent mechanism where each intersection continuously adjusts its timing parameters based on local performance metrics and neighbor information.
mechanism: Each intersection measures its own performance (vehicle throughput, queue length) and receives performance metrics from adjacent intersections. It then calculates a gradient indicating how to adjust green-split to improve its performance while considering neighbor performance. The adjustment is proportional to the local gradient and inversely proportional to the sum of neighbor performance metrics, creating a distributed optimization process.
evidence: Success of gradient-based optimization in other distributed systems
Empirical observation that traffic flow responds predictably to signal timing changes
Demonstration of similar principles in myxomycete tube networks
assumptions: Communication between adjacent intersections is reliable and timely
Performance metrics are sufficient to determine optimization direction
The system will converge to a global optimum through local adjustments
expected_failure_modes: Oscillations between intersections as they overcorrect based on neighbor information
Convergence to local maxima that are significantly worse than the global optimum
Sensitivity to measurement noise causing erratic timing adjustments
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis introduces a gradient-based approach to traffic signal control, which differs from traditional fixed-time or simple actuated control by using neighbor information to guide optimization direction, potentially avoiding local maxima traps.
testability: The hypothesis can be tested by implementing the algorithm in simulation and measuring convergence time, stability, and performance metrics. Variations in communication frequency and neighbor influence can be systematically tested.
falsifier: If the system consistently converges to suboptimal configurations even with perfect communication and sufficient iterations, or if it exhibits oscillatory behavior that doesn't dampen over time, the gradient descent mechanism would be falsified.
